title: Pardons Robert Cannon Hayes

The pardon appears among Trump's final clemency actions.
description_long: The Justice Department's register places Robert Cannon Hayes in its January 13, 2021 list of pardons. It identifies his case as a Western District of North Carolina matter and describes the offense as making false statements. The listed judgment, entered August 19, 2020, imposed one year of probation and a $9,500 fine. The register establishes the conviction, sentence, and later act of clemency; it does not explain the underlying statements, identify a victim, or give a reason for the pardon. That distinction matters: the available record supports describing what the government prosecuted and what Trump did, but not assigning a motive or assessing the merits of the case. A presidential pardon is a form of executive clemency tied to a federal offense; the listed action does not erase the historical fact that the conviction was entered. title: Restricts Travel from Iran Over COVID-19
description_short: Trump issued a proclamation suspending entry of certain travelers from Iran due to the coronavirus outbreak.
description_medium: On February 29, 2020, Trump issued a proclamation restricting entry for certain travelers who had been in Iran during the previous 14 days. The White House cited sustained person-to-person coronavirus transmission in Iran and added the country to travel limits that had first applied to China. The measure covered immigrant and nonimmigrant entry, subject to listed exceptions.
description_long: Trump's February 29, 2020 proclamation expanded the administration's early COVID-19 travel restrictions to Iran. It applied to noncitizens who had been physically present in Iran during the 14 days before seeking entry, whether as immigrants or nonimmigrants, with exceptions specified in the proclamation. The document said the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had determined that Iran was experiencing sustained person-to-person transmission. It cited 388 reported cases there as of February 28 and the CDC's highest travel alert, as well as reports that infections originating in Iran had appeared in 11 other countries. The proclamation framed the restriction as a response to the risk of imported cases and the capacity limits of public-health systems. It relied on presidential authority under immigration law and extended an earlier restriction focused on China. The document also included national-security language about Iran's reporting, a rationale separate from its discussion of disease transmission. The source records the administration's stated reasoning and the covered travel window; it does not by itself assess the measure's effectiveness or distinguish its public-health effects from its immigration consequences.

title: Poll: Checks and Balances Not Working Under Trump, Majority Says
description_short: A PBS News/NPR/Marist poll found two-thirds of Americans say checks and balances are not working well.
description_medium: A PBS News/NPR/Marist poll published February 23, 2026, found that about two-thirds of Americans said the system of checks and balances among the White House, Congress, and courts was not working well. That was 12 percentage points higher than a year earlier and double the December 2024 share. The article reported declining confidence among Democrats, independents, and Republicans.
description_long: The PBS News/NPR/Marist poll reported a sharp decline in public confidence in checks and balances during Trump's second term. About two-thirds of respondents said the system dividing authority among the White House, Congress, and courts was not working well. The article said that share had risen 12 percentage points from the same time in 2025 and doubled since December 2024, before Trump returned to office. The change crossed party lines: the report described especially large drops in confidence among Democrats and independents, as well as a 19-point decline among Republicans. The poll was published on February 23, 2026, shortly before the State of the Union address. The article presented the results as perceptions of how democratic institutions were functioning, not a direct measurement of institutional performance. It also discussed contemporary disputes over presidential authority and court decisions as relevant context, while noting that the poll preceded a major Supreme Court tariff ruling. The findings capture public opinion at a particular moment and should not be read as proof that checks had legally ceased to operate. They document a measurable rise in concern about the balance of power, including among voters in the president's own party.

description_long: The Trump administration backed away on October 23, 2025, from a planned federal immigration-enforcement operation in the San Francisco Bay Area. The plan had prompted opposition from California officials and protests near the base. Trump said he would not move forward after speaking with San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie and technology executives Marc Benioff and Jensen Huang. Lurie said Trump told him the deployment was being called off; Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem later reaffirmed that direction. The reversal came after demonstrators had mobilized, and federal vehicles encountered protesters outside the base. The report describes a canceled deployment rather than troops being sent into the city. title: Calls MS-13 Members "Animals" in Immigration Remarks
description_short: At a White House roundtable, Trump referred to MS-13 members as "animals" while discussing immigration enforcement.
description_medium: During a May 16, 2018, White House roundtable on California's sanctuary policies, Trump called people he described as gang members and immigrants “animals.” The remarks came amid a federal lawsuit challenging California laws that limited local cooperation with immigration enforcement. The phrasing drew criticism for dehumanizing language; the cited report situates it within the administration's broader dispute with the state.
description_long: At a May 16, 2018 White House meeting with California officials, Trump used the word “animals” while discussing people entering the country and those being removed by immigration authorities. The meeting focused on California's sanctuary policies and included officials who opposed the state's limits on local participation in federal immigration enforcement. The Justice Department had sued California in March, arguing that state laws conflicted with federal immigration policy. TIME reported the remarks and the political setting, including Trump's claim that the people being discussed were exceptionally dangerous. The article's headline identified the reference as involving deported gang members; the meeting remarks themselves moved from discussion of immigration and gang enforcement to the dehumanizing description. The language mattered because it blurred a distinction between alleged gang affiliation and immigrants more broadly, though the source does not establish that Trump intended every immigrant to be included. California Governor Jerry Brown publicly condemned the meeting and accused the president of misrepresenting immigration and crime. This account reports the wording, audience, and policy dispute without treating the remark as a formal immigration rule or a factual finding about any individual.

title: Fires Attorney General Jeff Sessions
description_short: Trump forced Attorney General Jeff Sessions to resign after months of pressure over the Russia probe.
description_medium: On November 7, 2018, Jeff Sessions resigned as attorney general at Trump's request, after months of presidential criticism over Sessions's recusal from the Russia investigation. The resignation came one day after the midterm elections. Trump appointed Sessions's chief of staff, Matthew Whitaker, as acting attorney general, raising questions about oversight of Special Counsel Robert Mueller's work.
description_long: Jeff Sessions left the attorney general's office on November 7, 2018, after Trump asked him to resign. Sessions had recused himself from overseeing the Russia investigation, and Trump had repeatedly criticized that decision. The departure came the day after the 2018 midterm elections, ending months of public tension between the president and the attorney general. Trump named Matthew Whitaker, who had been Sessions's chief of staff, as acting attorney general. Because the Justice Department supervised Special Counsel Robert Mueller's investigation, the leadership change drew attention to who would oversee the probe and whether its independence would be protected. The supplied CNBC report's title and summary confirm that Sessions resigned at Trump's request and connect the dispute to the Russia investigation. They do not establish that the resignation changed Mueller's findings or that Whitaker intervened in the investigation. This description therefore focuses on the personnel change, its timing, and the institutional question it raised. It does not equate Sessions's departure with a termination of the special counsel inquiry, which continued after he left office.

preserved_fields.title: Fires Attorney General Jeff Sessions
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump forced Attorney General Jeff Sessions to resign after months of pressure over the Russia probe.
